title: Yom HaShoah
hook: Holocaust Remembrance Day, in spring: candles lit and names read aloud

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Akiva's students, who died for not honoring each other. Your line was honor each other. Today, a newer day of mourning, inside the same weeks.

On one spring morning each year, a siren sounds across Israel and holds for two minutes. On highways, cars stop in the middle of the lanes, and drivers step out and stand beside them, still. In offices, people rise from their desks; in shops, the cashier stops mid-sale; children in schoolyards stand in rows. Then the siren fades, and people get back in their cars. Elsewhere in the world, in synagogues, schools and community halls, the day is kept differently, but often with the same two things: candles, and names.

segments.voice: Yom HaShoah is Holocaust Remembrance Day; in Israel its full name is the Day of Remembrance of the Holocaust and the Heroism. Shoah is a biblical word for devastation, a storm that destroys, and it's become the Hebrew name for the murder of six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. Israel's parliament set the day in 1951 and wrote it into law later that decade. It falls on the twenty-seventh of Nisan, less than a week after Passover ends. The date is tied to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which began on the eve of Passover, when Jews in the ghetto took up the few weapons they had against the German army. That's why the name includes heroism: remembering not only how people died, but how people resisted, in arms and in ordinary acts of keeping faith, keeping children alive, keeping names. The evening before, at Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem, survivors light six torches for the six million. In many places, names are read aloud, one after another, for hours, in a ceremony whose Hebrew name means every person has a name. Not every community marks this date. Some Haredi communities remember the Holocaust on traditional fast days instead, such as Tisha B'Av or the Tenth of Tevet, partly because Nisan is a month the tradition keeps for joy. The ways differ. What they share is a refusal to let the numbers erase the people. Six million is a figure no one can picture. A name, read aloud, is a person.
screen: `SHOAH: DEVASTATION.` · `THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OF NISAN.` · `THE HOLOCAUST AND THE HEROISM.` · `EVERY PERSON HAS A NAME.` · then, large: `REMEMBER IN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, safely, or picture its flame, and stay silent. If you know the name of someone who died in the Holocaust, from your family, your community, or a story you've read, hold that name; if not, hold the fact that each of the six million had one.
Yom HaShoah. Holocaust Remembrance Day: candles, a siren, and names read aloud. Today's word.
Your line: remember in silence. Some days ask for nothing more than that. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, the twenty-seventh of Nisan, Israel stops for a two-minute siren, and communities around the world hold ceremonies with memorial candles, survivors' testimony, the reading of names, Kaddish and the memorial prayer El Malei Rachamim.
